scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's full-frame schematic island and exact colour map. Blue means shallow beaks, yellow means middle beaks, and green means deep beaks. White marks barriers and breeding tests. The title appears briefly, then clears while the mixed flock keeps moving.

scenes.tts: The first film showed inherited beak differences spreading through unequal reproductive success. When does one changing population become two species? Start with one mixed finch population. Its members can meet, breed, and exchange gene versions across the island.
scenes.caption: The first film showed inherited beak differences spreading through unequal reproductive success. When does one changing population become two species? Start with one mixed finch population. Its members can meet, breed, and exchange gene versions across the island.
scenes.visual: Carry the mixed blue, yellow, and green flock from the first film. Paired birds exchange small labelled gene blocks through moving white arrows. A white bracket labels the whole connected flock 'one population'. No molecular structures.
scenes.narration: The first film showed inherited beak differences spreading through unequal reproductive success. When does one changing population become two species? Start with one mixed finch population. Its members can meet, breed, and exchange gene versions across the island.

scenes.tts: Biologists often use interbreeding as the test. A species includes populations whose members interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring. They rarely breed with other groups. This biological species concept applies to sexual organisms, and its edges can be fuzzy.
scenes.caption: Biologists often use interbreeding as the test. A species includes populations whose members interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring. They rarely breed with other groups. This biological species concept applies to sexual organisms, and its edges can be fuzzy.
scenes.visual: Turn the exchange arrows into a simple breeding bridge between moving bird pairs. Offspring tokens cross the bridge and later pair again, showing fertile offspring without labels of certainty. Place 'biological species concept' above the bridge and 'sexual organisms' below.
scenes.narration: Biologists often use interbreeding as the test. A species includes populations whose members interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring. They rarely breed with other groups. This biological species concept applies to sexual organisms, and its edges can be fuzzy.

scenes.tts: Now a river divides the habitat. Birds on opposite sides meet less often, so gene flow falls. The river creates geographic isolation. Has the river already made two species, or has it only started a possible split? Make your prediction.
scenes.caption: Now a river divides the habitat. Birds on opposite sides meet less often, so gene flow falls. The river creates geographic isolation. Has the river already made two species, or has it only started a possible split? Make your prediction.
scenes.visual: A wide white-edged river grows through the carried island. Exchange arrows across it thin and fade, but do not label them zero. Keep mixed colours on both banks. End with the prediction question spanning the river.
scenes.narration: Now a river divides the habitat. Birds on opposite sides meet less often, so gene flow falls. The river creates geographic isolation. Has the river already made two species, or has it only started a possible split? Make your prediction.

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction question over the divided island. Water flows and birds move within each bank. No species labels or answer symbols appear.

scenes.tts: Separation alone is not speciation. On the day the river appears, the birds may still breed if they meet. Distance describes where the groups are. The species test asks what happens when their members meet and try to reproduce.
scenes.caption: Separation alone is not speciation. On the day the river appears, the birds may still breed if they meet. Distance describes where the groups are. The species test asks what happens when their members meet and try to reproduce.
scenes.visual: Place two large gauges beside the island: 'distance' and 'interbreeding test'. The distance gauge changes when the river appears; the interbreeding gauge stays marked 'not tested'. Move one pair toward a temporary white bridge without revealing an outcome.
scenes.narration: Separation alone is not speciation. On the day the river appears, the birds may still breed if they meet. Distance describes where the groups are. The species test asks what happens when their members meet and try to reproduce.

scenes.tts: Across many generations, different mutations may arise on each side. Different conditions may favour different inherited traits. Chance can shift small groups too. The two colour distributions may move apart while reduced gene flow keeps differences from mixing freely.
scenes.caption: Across many generations, different mutations may arise on each side. Different conditions may favour different inherited traits. Chance can shift small groups too. The two colour distributions may move apart while reduced gene flow keeps differences from mixing freely.
scenes.visual: Show a schematic generation slider moving forward with no spoken numbers. Label both distributions 'schematic'. The left bank slowly trends bluer and the right bank greener, but both retain mixed colours. Mutation blocks appear occasionally; a small chance spinner nudges either distribution.
scenes.narration: Across many generations, different mutations may arise on each side. Different conditions may favour different inherited traits. Chance can shift small groups too. The two colour distributions may move apart while reduced gene flow keeps differences from mixing freely.

scenes.tts: Gene flow moves gene versions between populations when individuals, or sex cells such as pollen, arrive and add their genes. Before the river, that mixing can keep the groups connected. After isolation, less mixing lets differences build more easily. Reduced gene flow allows divergence; it does not prove that divergence or speciation occurred.
scenes.caption: Gene flow moves gene versions between populations when individuals, or sex cells such as pollen, arrive and add their genes. Before the river, that mixing can keep the groups connected. After isolation, less mixing lets differences build more easily. Reduced gene flow allows divergence; it does not prove that divergence or speciation occurred.
scenes.visual: Rewind the schematic island briefly. Before isolation, bird tokens and labelled gene blocks (one drifting like windblown pollen) cross the future river line. Restore the river and reduce, but do not erase, those arrows. Place 'reduced gene flow' above the gap and keep the interbreeding gauge marked 'not yet tested'.
scenes.narration: Gene flow moves gene versions between populations when individuals, or sex cells such as pollen, arrive and add their genes. Before the river, that mixing can keep the groups connected. After isolation, less mixing lets differences build more easily. Reduced gene flow allows divergence; it does not prove that divergence or speciation occurred.

scenes.tts: Within each group, the same selection rule still works. Inherited traits spread when their carriers leave more reproducing offspring. The environment can make different traits helpful on each side. This can support divergence, but selection does not define the species boundary.
scenes.caption: Within each group, the same selection rule still works. Inherited traits spread when their carriers leave more reproducing offspring. The environment can make different traits helpful on each side. This can support divergence, but selection does not define the species boundary.
scenes.visual: Run parent-to-offspring arrows within both banks using the shared colour map. Center the guiding rule briefly across both groups. Then move it upward and highlight the separate 'interbreeding test' gauge to show that selection and the species test are different.
scenes.narration: Within each group, the same selection rule still works. Inherited traits spread when their carriers leave more reproducing offspring. The environment can make different traits helpful on each side. This can support divergence, but selection does not define the species boundary.

scenes.tts: Imagine the barrier disappears. If the groups interbreed regularly and exchange genes, the split is incomplete under this concept. If barriers prevent interbreeding, or allow only rare hybrids, the groups count as separate species. That is reproductive isolation.
scenes.caption: Imagine the barrier disappears. If the groups interbreed regularly and exchange genes, the split is incomplete under this concept. If barriers prevent interbreeding, or allow only rare hybrids, the groups count as separate species. That is reproductive isolation.
scenes.visual: Lower the river while preserving the two schematic distributions. Send neutral dotted meeting paths between groups. Split the frame into conditional outcomes labelled 'interbreed regularly' and 'no interbreeding, or only rare hybrids'. Do not show rejection, extinction, or guaranteed failure.
scenes.narration: Imagine the barrier disappears. If the groups interbreed regularly and exchange genes, the split is incomplete under this concept. If barriers prevent interbreeding, or allow only rare hybrids, the groups count as separate species. That is reproductive isolation.

scenes.tts: Real boundaries can remain fuzzy. Some named species hybridise occasionally, and the concept does not fit organisms reproducing without sex. Speciation can also begin without a barrier. The river is one useful model, not a rule that every lineage follows.
scenes.caption: Real boundaries can remain fuzzy. Some named species hybridise occasionally, and the concept does not fit organisms reproducing without sex. Speciation can also begin without a barrier. The river is one useful model, not a rule that every lineage follows.
scenes.visual: Soften the boundary between the conditional outcomes. Let one dotted path cross under 'occasionally' without changing either group's label. Slide the river model into one card among several blank schematic route cards, keeping all uncertain routes neutral.
scenes.narration: Real boundaries can remain fuzzy. Some named species hybridise occasionally, and the concept does not fit organisms reproducing without sex. Speciation can also begin without a barrier. The river is one useful model, not a rule that every lineage follows.

scenes.tts: So a barrier can start a split by reducing gene flow. Mutation, selection, and chance may then make populations diverge. Interbreeding tests whether the split is complete. The same mechanism that changes populations can help separate them across generations.
scenes.caption: So a barrier can start a split by reducing gene flow. Mutation, selection, and chance may then make populations diverge. Interbreeding tests whether the split is complete. The same mechanism that changes populations can help separate them across generations.
scenes.visual: Transform the island sequence into a moving three-step path: reduced gene flow, possible divergence, interbreeding test. Keep 'may diverge' over the middle step. Finish on the two gauges, with the barrier pointing toward the interbreeding test rather than replacing it.
scenes.narration: So a barrier can start a split by reducing gene flow. Mutation, selection, and chance may then make populations diverge. Interbreeding tests whether the split is complete. The same mechanism that changes populations can help separate them across generations.

scenes.visual: Show one line only, large and centered: 'A barrier can start a split; interbreeding tests whether it is complete.' No subtitle, title, logo, or smaller line.
